title: Introduction to Statistics
summary: Learn to describe data with tables, graphs, averages and spread, then meet probability, the normal distribution and the importance of fair samples.
audience: Secondary and university students who need the basic ideas of statistics for exams, projects or everyday decisions

lessons.title: Populations, samples and types of data

body.p: Statistics is the science of learning from data. A population is the whole group you want to know about, for example all 600 students in a school in Accra. A sample is a smaller part of that group that you actually study, for example 30 students. We usually study a sample because asking everyone costs too much time and money. We then use the sample to make a careful guess about the population.

A sample is only useful if it is fair. Imagine a teacher in Nairobi who wants to know how long students spend travelling to school. If she only asks the students who sit in the front row, she may miss students who arrive late after long journeys. That sample is biased. The best way to avoid bias is random sampling, where every member of the population has an equal chance of being chosen, for example by drawing names from a bag.
Data is the information we collect. Each piece of information about a person or thing is a variable. Variables come in two main kinds, and each kind has two types.

list: Categorical data puts things into groups. Nominal categories have no order, such as eye colour, home language or favourite sport. Ordinal categories have a natural order, such as 'poor, fair, good, excellent'.
Numerical data is measured or counted. Discrete data is counted in whole steps, such as the number of siblings (0, 1, 2, 3) or the number of goals in a match.

Continuous data can take any value in a range, such as height in centimetres, time in seconds or mass in kilograms. Measurements are continuous because a more accurate tool could always give more decimal places.

body.p: Worked example: a class in Lusaka is asked three questions. 'Which subject do you like best?' gives nominal categorical data. 'How many books did you read this term?' gives discrete numerical data. 'How tall are you?' gives continuous numerical data. Knowing the type matters because it decides which graphs and calculations make sense. You can find the mean of heights, but you cannot find the mean of home languages.

body.tip: A quick test: if you could sensibly add the values together, the data is numerical. A phone number is made of digits but adding two phone numbers means nothing, so it is categorical.

body.p: Raw data is hard to read. A frequency table organises it by showing how many times each value or category appears. The count is called the frequency. Suppose 20 students were asked how they travel to school. The answers, written as a list, were: walk 8 times, bus 6 times, bike 3 times and car 3 times (this is made-up practice data). The frequency table is below. The relative frequency is the frequency divided by the total, shown as a percentage.

body.code:
Transport   Frequency   Relative frequency
Walk             8          8/20 = 40%
Bus              6          6/20 = 30%
Bike             3          3/20 = 15%
Car              3          3/20 = 15%
Total           20          100%

body.p: Always check that the frequencies add up to the number of people you asked and that the percentages add to 100. This simple check catches many counting mistakes.

list: A bar chart is for categorical data. Draw a gap between the bars because the categories are separate. The height of each bar is the frequency.
A histogram is for continuous numerical data that has been put into groups such as 150 to 159 cm. The bars touch because the groups follow on from each other with no gaps.
A pie chart shows how a whole splits into parts. The walk group above takes 40% of the circle, which is 0.40 x 360 = 144 degrees.
A line graph shows how one value changes over time, such as a town's rainfall each month.

body.p: Here is a simple text bar chart of the transport table. Each star stands for one student.

A good graph has a title, labelled axes with units, and an honest scale. A bar chart whose vertical axis starts at 50 instead of 0 makes small differences look huge. When you read someone else's graph, always look at the axis first.

body.tip: When you group continuous data, make every group the same width, and make sure each value fits in exactly one group. Write 150 to under 160, then 160 to under 170, so that a student of exactly 160 cm is not counted twice.

body.p: An average is a single number that describes the centre of a data set. There are three common averages, and each answers a slightly different question. We will use ten quiz marks out of 10 from a class: 4, 6, 7, 7, 8, 8, 8, 9, 9, 10.

list: Mean: add all the values and divide by how many there are. The sum is 76 and there are 10 marks, so the mean is 76 / 10 = 7.6.

Median: the middle value when the data is in order. With 10 values there are two middle ones, the 5th and 6th, which are 8 and 8. Their average is 8, so the median is 8. With an odd number of values, the median is the single middle one.

Mode: the value that appears most often. The mark 8 appears three times, more than any other, so the mode is 8. A data set can have two modes, or none if every value appears once. The mode is the only average that works for categories, such as the most popular sport.

body.p: The mean uses every value, so one extreme value can drag it a long way. Nine students in Kampala are asked their weekly pocket money, and the answers are 5, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10, 12 and 15 (in local currency units). The mean is about 8.56 and the median is 8. Now a tenth student who receives 90 joins the group. The mean jumps to 16.7, higher than nine of the ten students, while the median only moves to 8.5.

This is why news reports about incomes and house prices often use the median. A few very rich people raise the mean but barely change the median. An unusually high or low value is called an outlier. When data has outliers or is strongly lopsided, the median describes a typical person better. When the data is fairly balanced, the mean is a good choice because it uses all the information.

body.tip: Always put the data in order before finding the median. Forgetting this is the most common mistake in the topic.

body.p: Check your understanding: for 3, 5, 8, 12 and 2, the mean is 30 / 5 = 6. In order the data is 2, 3, 5, 8, 12, so the median is 5. They are different, and both are correct answers to different questions.

lessons.title: Range, quartiles and the interquartile range

body.p: Two classes can have the same average and still be very different. One class may have marks that are all close together, while the other has some very high and some very low marks. A measure of spread tells us how far apart the values are.

The simplest measure is the range: the largest value minus the smallest. For the data 3, 5, 8, 9, 11, 12, 14 and 6 (which in order is 3, 5, 6, 8, 9, 11, 12, 14), the range is 14 - 3 = 11. The range is easy to find but it depends only on two values, so one outlier changes it completely.

Quartiles split ordered data into four equal parts. The median is the second quartile, Q2. The lower quartile Q1 is the median of the lower half, and the upper quartile Q3 is the median of the upper half. The method in this course is: find the median, split the data into a lower half and an upper half (leaving out the median itself if the number of values is odd), then find the median of each half.
The interquartile range (IQR) is Q3 minus Q1. It tells you how wide the middle half of the data is, and it ignores the extreme values at both ends. Here the IQR is 6.

A second example with an odd number of values: 2, 4, 5, 7, 8, 10, 13. The median is 7. Leaving out 7, the lower half is 2, 4, 5 so Q1 = 4, and the upper half is 8, 10, 13 so Q3 = 10. The IQR is 10 - 4 = 6.

body.tip: Calculators and software such as Excel can use slightly different quartile methods, so their answers may differ a little from the method above, especially for small data sets. In an exam, use the method your teacher or syllabus requires.

body.p: A common rule of thumb calls a value an outlier if it lies more than 1.5 x IQR below Q1 or above Q3. For the second example, 1.5 x 6 = 9, so the limits are 4 - 9 = -5 and 10 + 9 = 19. A value of 25 would be flagged as an outlier.

The standard deviation measures how far values typically lie from the mean. A small standard deviation means the values cluster close to the mean. A large one means they are widely scattered. It uses every value, which makes it the most common measure of spread with the mean.

body.h: The population formula step by step

steps: Find the mean of the data.
Subtract the mean from each value to get the deviations.
Square each deviation, so that negatives do not cancel positives.
Divide by n, the number of values. This gives the variance.
Take the square root of the variance. This gives the standard deviation.

body.p: Worked example: eight students record the hours they study in a week: 2, 4, 4, 4, 5, 5, 7, 9. The sum is 40, so the mean is 40 / 8 = 5.

body.code:
Value  Deviation (x - 5)  Squared
  2         -3                9
  4         -1                1
  4         -1                1
  4         -1                1
  5          0                0
  5          0                0
  7          2                4
  9          4               16
Sum of squares = 32
Variance = 32 / 8 = 4
Standard deviation = sqrt(4) = 2 hours

body.p: The standard deviation is 2 hours, in the same units as the data. Notice that the deviations add to zero, which is why we square them first. Another check: for the data 3, 5, 6, 8, 9, 11, 12, 14 the mean is 8.5, the variance is 12.25 and the standard deviation is 3.5.

Now compare two small classes with the same mean. Class A scored 48, 50, 52, 50, 50 and Class B scored 20, 80, 35, 65, 50. Both have a mean of 50. Class A has a standard deviation of about 1.26 and Class B about 21.21. The tiny first number tells us Class A is very consistent, and the large second number tells us Class B is scattered.

body.tip: This lesson uses the population formula, which divides by n, because we treat the data as the whole group. When the data is a sample used to estimate a bigger population, many textbooks and calculators divide by n - 1 instead. Check which one your course expects. The idea is the same.

body.p: The standard deviation is never negative, and it equals zero only when every value is identical.

Probability measures how likely an event is. It is a number from 0 to 1. A probability of 0 means the event is impossible, 1 means it is certain, and 0.5 means it is equally likely to happen or not. When all outcomes are equally likely, the probability of an event is the number of favourable outcomes divided by the total number of outcomes.

A fair six-sided die has six outcomes: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 and 6. The event 'an even number' has three favourable outcomes (2, 4 and 6), so P(even) = 3/6 = 1/2. A bag holds 5 red, 3 blue and 2 green counters, 10 in all. Picking one at random, P(blue) = 3/10 = 0.3.

The complement of an event is 'the event does not happen'. Since something must happen, the two probabilities add to 1, so P(not A) = 1 - P(A). On a die, P(6) = 1/6, therefore P(not 6) = 1 - 1/6 = 5/6. If a weather office says the chance of rain is 0.3, the chance of no rain is 1 - 0.3 = 0.7.
Events that cannot happen together are called mutually exclusive. For these we add the probabilities. In the bag, P(red or blue) = 5/10 + 3/10 = 8/10 = 0.8.

Two events are independent if one does not change the chance of the other. A coin toss does not affect a die roll. For independent events, multiply: P(A and B) = P(A) x P(B). So P(heads and a 6) = 1/2 x 1/6 = 1/12. Rolling two dice, P(both are 6) = 1/6 x 1/6 = 1/36, which is about 0.028.
The phrase 'at least one' is easier with the complement. The chance of at least one 6 in two rolls is 1 - P(no 6 in either roll) = 1 - (5/6 x 5/6) = 1 - 25/36 = 11/36, which is about 0.306.

body.tip: The coin has no memory. After five heads in a row, the next toss is still 1/2 for heads. Believing otherwise is called the gambler's fallacy.

lessons.title: The normal distribution and why sample size matters

body.p: Many measurements, such as adult heights in a large population or errors in careful measuring, form a pattern that rises to a peak in the middle and falls away evenly on both sides. This bell-shaped pattern is called a normal distribution. It is symmetrical, so the mean, median and mode are all at the centre. Not all data is normal, so we should not assume it without looking at it. Income data, for example, is usually lopsided.

For data that is approximately normal, with mean m and standard deviation s, the following holds roughly. About 68% of values lie within 1 standard deviation of the mean, about 95% within 2, and about 99.7% within 3. Software gives these more precisely as 68.27%, 95.45% and 99.73%.
Example: suppose marks on a large test are approximately normal with mean 60 and standard deviation 10.

body.code:
Within 1 sd: 60 +/- 10  -> 50 to 70   about 68%
Within 2 sd: 60 +/- 20  -> 40 to 80   about 95%
Within 3 sd: 60 +/- 30  -> 30 to 90   about 99.7%
Above 80: the other 5% is split evenly into two tails -> about 2.5%

body.p: So a mark of 80 is unusually high, since only about 2.5% of students score higher. A mark of 85 would be even rarer. This is how the standard deviation lets us judge whether a value is ordinary or unusual.

A sample mean will not match the population mean exactly. Different random samples give different means. With a larger random sample, the sample mean varies less from sample to sample. If the population standard deviation is 10, the typical size of that variation is 10 divided by the square root of n. For n = 25 it is 10 / 5 = 2, for n = 100 it is 10 / 10 = 1, and for n = 400 it is 10 / 20 = 0.5. Quadrupling the sample size halves the typical error.

A bigger sample cannot repair a biased one. A phone survey that only reaches people who own phones is biased however many calls are made. Good conclusions need a fair, random sample and a sensible size.

body.tip: Be careful with claims such as 'a survey of 5 people shows...'. A very small sample can easily give a result that is far from the truth, even when it is chosen fairly.

quiz.q: A teacher wants to know how many of the 600 students in her school walk to school. She asks 40 students chosen by drawing names from a bag. What are the 40 students called?
options: A sample
The population
A variable
A frequency

quiz.q: Which of these is continuous numerical data?
options: The number of goals scored in a match
The home language of a student
The time, in seconds, that a runner takes to finish 100 m
A satisfaction rating of poor, fair, good or excellent

quiz.q: A survey of 20 students finds that 6 travel by bus. What is the relative frequency of bus travel as a percentage?
Which graph is most suitable for showing how many students chose each of five favourite sports?
options: A line graph over time
A histogram with touching bars
A scatter of the median values
A bar chart with gaps between the bars

quiz.q: What are the mean and median of the data 3, 5, 8, 12, 2?
options: Mean 5 and median 6
Mean 6 and median 8
Mean 30 and median 5
Mean 6 and median 5

quiz.q: Nine students have weekly pocket money of 5, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10, 12 and 15. A tenth student with 90 joins. Which statement is correct?
options: The median rises more than the mean
The mean rises a lot, from about 8.56 to 16.7, but the median only changes from 8 to 8.5
Neither the mean nor the median changes
The mode rises to 90

quiz.q: Find the interquartile range of 3, 5, 6, 8, 9, 11, 12, 14 using the median-of-each-half method.
Why is the interquartile range often preferred to the range when data may contain outliers?
options: It always gives a smaller answer than the standard deviation
It uses every value in the data set
It measures only the middle half of the data, so extreme values do not affect it
It is the same as the mean deviation

quiz.q: Class A and Class B both have a mean mark of 50. Class A has a standard deviation of 1.3 and Class B has a standard deviation of 21.2. What does this tell you?
options: Class B marks are much more spread out than Class A marks
Class A marks are much more spread out than Class B marks
Class B has the higher average mark
Class A has more students

quiz.q: What is the population standard deviation of the data 3, 3, 7, 7?
The probability of rain tomorrow is 0.3. What is the probability that it does not rain?
A fair coin is tossed and a fair die is rolled. What is the probability of getting tails and a 6?
A bag contains 5 red, 3 blue and 2 green counters. One is picked at random. What is the probability that it is red or blue?
Test marks are approximately normal with mean 60 and standard deviation 10. Roughly what percentage of students score between 40 and 80?
options: About 68%
About 99.7%
About 95%
About 50%

quiz.q: A school wants to estimate average study time using a random sample. What is the main effect of using a larger random sample?
options: The sample mean is likely to be closer to the population mean
The sample mean will always equal the population mean exactly
Any bias in how the sample was chosen disappears
The standard deviation of the population becomes zero
